posture: One distinct new NSW signal in week three of the reformed regime: the Industrial Relations Commission has handed down its first published stop-bullying decision, refusing to strike out parts of a worker's application even though some alleged conduct occurred away from work. It is an interlocutory, preventive-jurisdiction ruling rather than a workers-comp claim determination, so it sits at watch, but it is the first precedent in the IRC's expanded bullying jurisdiction and reads across to how the reformed scheme's psychological-injury conduct claims will be framed. Otherwise NSW's primary regulators (SIRA, icare, Personal Injury Commission, SafeWork NSW) produced no fresh, non-duplicative release, and no interstate or national item cleared the jurisdiction-weighting bar.
summary: A near-quiet day with a single carry-worthy legal signal. The NSW IRC issued what is reported as its first published decision in the stop-bullying jurisdiction it acquired in October 2025, declining to remove non-work allegations because they may bear on the risk of future bullying — an early read on the 'at work' boundary in that jurisdiction. All other NSW regulator and tribunal channels returned only commencement-day reform background already covered in the 28 June – 14 July digests, which is not repeated. Interstate and national activity (Comcare's 1 July statutory-rate refresh, the Queensland scheme review due late 2026, and the frozen Victorian/Queensland/SA premium settings) was routine or already captured, and no verifiable fresh AFR or SMH public headline on Australian workers compensation surfaced.

items.headline: NSW Industrial Relations Commission delivers its first published stop-bullying decision, keeping non-work conduct in play
items.summary: In what is reported as the IRC's first published decision under the stop-bullying and sexual-harassment jurisdiction it gained in October 2025, Commissioner Muir declined to strike out parts of an executive assistant's application against a regional council and an individual councillor, even though he accepted some of the alleged conduct did not occur while she was 'at work'. The reasoning was that the non-work allegations could still be relevant to assessing the prospect of future bullying.
items.so_what: As the first precedent on the reach of the IRC's bullying jurisdiction, it signals a broad reading of what conduct can be examined — relevant because the same Commission is the new gateway for contested psychological-injury workers-comp claims under the July reforms, so an expansive 'at work' and future-risk approach here could shape how bullying-based psychological-injury disputes are framed and defended.
